_note: Frozen content for design review. Specimen family — one enormous phrase per sheet against small technical annotations on hairlines. Black on white, one weight pair, no third colour. The closer reverses.

slots.annotation: On the line that decides whether the rest gets read
slots.item1: Six headlines pulled apart, and the rule each one is obeying.
slots.item2: A formula. Every one of these fails somewhere obvious.
slots.coverNote: The last specimen is the one that breaks the other five

slots.body: A headline about improving your workflow contains no information. A headline about the four minutes you lose every time you switch tabs contains all of it. The specific version is harder to write and immediately easier to believe.
slots.v1: The actual thing, not the class of things it belongs to.
slots.v2: One concrete particular does more than three adjectives.
slots.v3: Workflow, process, strategy — words that hold the space where meaning goes.

slots.body: The line has to leave something open, because a complete statement gives the reader everything and no reason to continue. The tension has to be genuine, though — an opening that promises more than the piece contains is the fastest way to lose somebody permanently.
slots.v1: Exactly one. Two unresolved things read as vagueness, not intrigue.
slots.v2: The gap you open must close, on that page, without a detour.
slots.v3: A line the piece cannot honour costs you the next five as well.

slots.body: Cutting a headline to four words often removes the detail that made it worth reading. The correct length is however long the specific claim takes, and a nine-word line that says something beats a four-word line that gestures.
slots.v1: Not words. A short line carrying nothing is not economical.
slots.v2: Articles and prepositions go first, and nothing is lost.
slots.v3: If they carry no meaning alone, the line starts in the wrong place.

slots.body: Emphasis sits at the end of a line, which is where a reader's attention stops rather than where it starts. Rearranging a sentence so the surprising word finishes it is the single cheapest edit available to any headline.
slots.v1: The concrete one. Never end on a qualifier or an adverb.
slots.v2: Most weak lines contain the right word in the wrong position.
slots.v3: Whatever you stress out loud should be the last thing on the line.

slots.annotation: Register — the voice it is written in
slots.body: Headlines drift into an announcement voice nobody uses in conversation, and the drift is invisible to the person doing it. The test is whether you could say the line out loud to a colleague — if it would be strange to say, it is strange to read.
slots.v1: Out loud, in the room. The embarrassing ones are obvious immediately.
slots.v2: Introducing, unveiling, excited to share. Nobody speaks like this.
slots.v3: The way you order a sentence in speech is usually the clearer order.

slots.body: Everything above makes the opening better at getting somebody to read the next paragraph, and none of it makes the next paragraph worth reading. Time spent on the headline is the most visible work available and rarely the most useful.
slots.v1: You cannot name what the piece is until the piece exists.
slots.v2: Past that you are avoiding the part that actually needs work.
slots.v3: It is doing more of the work and gets none of the attention.

slots.annotation: On whatever you are about to publish
slots.closingLine: One edit, thirty seconds, no new writing. It is the only thing on this list that works every time.
slots.signoff: Then go and fix the second line
